slides.title: East regional distribution center: close in 2027, or retain and optimize?

paragraphs.text: NORTHLINE HOME  |  CEO AND BOARD DECISION PAPER
East regional distribution center: close in 2027, or retain and optimize?
Recommendation: retain and optimize East through its 2029 lease end, and use 2027–28 to test the cross-dock alternative before the lease decision
Based only on the board briefing pack (synthetic case data). All figures are in US$, at 2027 volumes unless stated.

slides.title: Executive summary: retain and optimize East through its 2029 lease end. Neither closure option both saves money and meets the board's 2027 constraints

paragraphs.text: Executive summary: retain and optimize East through its 2029 lease end. Neither closure option both saves money and meets the board's 2027 constraints

Governing thought: Keep East in 2027 and optimize it (Option K: saves $0.30M a year for $0.15M one-time), and run a capped cross-dock test. Closing East saves at most $0.10M a year, not the $1.3M claimed, and fails or cannot yet prove the SLA, capacity and evidence tests. The 2029 lease end is the real decision point.
Closing East does not pay once routing and handling are counted

The CFO's $1.3M is East's gross fixed cost. Serving 200k Eastern orders from Central adds $1.0M of transport (200k × $5) and $0.2M of damage: a net $0.10M a year, zero at 2028 volume, before the $0.75M exit fee
The cross-dock costs $0.15M a year more than today: $3 extra per order ($0.60M) outweighs the $0.45M fixed-cost reduction
Optimized retention (K) is the cheapest design in the base case: $8.44M in 2027, $0.20–0.45M a year below either closure
Closure also breaks, or cannot yet prove, the board's binding constraints

Close to Central: 90.3% network two-day rate vs the 92% contract; Central at 100% of capacity in 2027 and 108% in 2028; the $1.1M retrofit it needs is unbudgeted and would take one-time spend to $1.85M vs $0.9M authorized
Cross-dock: 93.9% on paper, but from a 6-week, non-holiday pilot with no all-ZIP definition and no promotion guarantee
Retain and optimize: 95.1% network rate, Central at 47% in 2028, $0.15M one-time
Optimize now, test the cross-dock, and decide the 2029 lease at a Q3 2028 gate
Approve Option K and a capped cross-dock test (≤$0.25M) through holiday 2027 and spring 2028, measured on all ZIP codes
Waiting avoids the $0.75M early-exit fee and settles whether the $0.85M minimum is extra or credited; that point swings the cross-dock's cost by $0.85M a year
Drop close-to-Central: its $5-per-order penalty makes it no cheaper than today at 2028 volume, even if Central were expanded
Source: Northline Home briefing pack (synthetic case data), sections 2–7; Northline analysis.

slides.title: We tested four network designs and a deferral path against the board's four tests plus reversibility, using all-in cost and the contracted all-ZIP service KPI

paragraphs.text: We tested four network designs and a deferral path against the board's four tests plus reversibility, using all-in cost and the contracted all-ZIP service KPI
FIVE TESTS: FOUR SET BY THE BOARD, PLUS REVERSIBILITY
Keep all three sites as they are today. This is the reference case
Lowest all-in annual cost: transport, facility fixed cost and damage, plus one-time cost. Not the CFO's carrier-only cost per shipment
Renegotiate East staffing shifts and add a transfer buffer for low-volume SKUs. Saves $0.30M a year for $0.15M upfront (facility audit)
At least 92% of all orders delivered within two days, network-wide, on all ZIP codes (the contracted KPI, not the ex-rural dashboard)
End the East lease in 2027 ($0.75M) and ship all 200k Eastern orders from Central at $13 each
Central at or below its 360k certified practical capacity in 2027 and under 2028 growth (+10% East, +6% Central)
End the East lease and sign a two-year deal with a third-party Eastern cross-dock: $11 per order plus a $0.85M annual minimum
No more than $0.9M of one-time change cost in 2027; East early exit $0.75M; West lease fixed to 2030
Decision-grade evidence and reversibility (rebuilding East-type capacity takes nine months)
Run K now, test the cross-dock through holiday peak, and decide at the 2029 lease end

Burden of proof: closing East is hard to reverse (nine months plus customer migrations) and must pass all five tests on today's evidence. Where the evidence is incomplete, we say so and treat it as a risk, not a pass.
Source: Northline Home briefing pack (synthetic case data), sections 2, 3, 6.

slides.title: Our working hypothesis, the CEO's 'keep East open in 2027', held up under testing, but it needed three refinements

paragraphs.text: Our working hypothesis, the CEO's 'keep East open in 2027', held up under testing, but it needed three refinements
WHAT WOULD HAVE TO BE TRUE FOR 'KEEP EAST' TO BE RIGHT, AND WHAT WE FOUND
Keep East open in 2027, because Central has too little spare capacity for demand growth.
a  Closing saves little once all costs are counted
Close to Central nets $0.10M a year (vs $1.3M claimed) and $0 at 2028 volume; the cross-dock costs $0.15M a year more than today (slides 6–8)
1  Retain and optimize, not just retain. Option K beats the status quo by $0.30M a year at low risk.
2  Capacity only rules out close-to-Central. The cross-dock fails on cost ($0.45M a year above K in the base case) and on unproven peak service.
3  Keep East through 2029, not permanently. The early-exit fee falls away at lease end. Test the cross-dock now and decide at a Q3 2028 gate.
b  Closing puts the 92% SLA at risk
Close to Central: 90.3% (fail). Cross-dock: 93.9% on paper, from non-peak pilot data (slides 9–10)
c  Central cannot absorb Eastern demand
True for close to Central: 108% of capacity in 2028. Not relevant to the cross-dock, which does not use Central (slide 11)
d  Keeping East fits the lease and budget
Lease runs to 2029 with no fee; K needs $0.15M of the $0.9M authorized (slide 12)
e  Keeping East is the cheapest way to meet the SLA
Yes: even unoptimized, East ($8.74M) beats the only SLA-compliant closure option ($8.89M). K is cheaper still at $8.44M (slide 7)
Source: Northline Home briefing pack (synthetic case data), sections 2–7; Northline analysis.

slides.title: Five claims in the board pre-read overstate the case for one side or the other and should not anchor the decision

paragraphs.text: Five claims in the board pre-read overstate the case for one side or the other and should not anchor the decision
Counts East's fixed cost only. Leaves out the higher Central-to-East transport (+$5 × 200k), $0.2M extra damage and the $0.75M exit fee
$0.10M a year before the $0.75M exit fee (–$0.65M in 2027); $0 at 2028 volume
Cost per shipment as the cost KPI
Carrier invoice ÷ orders; excludes warehouse rent, returns and replacements, so it is a transport KPI only
Use all-in cost: $8.44–8.89M a year by option
Excludes rural deliveries; the contract KPI counts every ZIP code
Correlation only. East serves more high-volume accounts with dedicated sales teams, and this is not controlled for
Not usable as causal evidence; retention response to service is unknown
“Close in June 2027 and absorb at Central with today's staffing”
Puts Central at its full 360k practical load before any demand spike; 2028 growth takes it past capacity

Implication: these corrections cut both ways. They remove most of the closure saving (CFO, consultant) and also the inflated service and loyalty case for keeping East (Finance, Marketing). The decision rests on the corrected figures.
Source: Northline Home briefing pack (synthetic case data), sections 3, 5. Corrected figures: Northline analysis.

slides.title: After routing and damage costs, the CFO's $1.3M closure saving shrinks to $0.10M a year, and to zero at 2028 volume

paragraphs.text: After routing and damage costs, the CFO's $1.3M closure saving shrinks to $0.10M a year, and to zero at 2028 volume
Option C (close East, serve from Central): annual saving vs status quo, $M
Fixed cost removed: East site $1.30M a year
Damage: +$0.20M a year for transshipped goods
Break-even volume: $1.10M ÷ $5 = 220k Eastern orders, exactly the 2028 forecast
NOT YET INCLUDED: ALL MAKE IT WORSE
$0.75M exit fee: 7.5-year payback at $0.10M a year, for a lease that ends in 2029 anyway
Carrier surcharge needed to lift Eastern service above 84% (not priced)
$1.1M Central retrofit needed once 2028 growth arrives (slide 11)
Compared with Option K, close-to-Central is $0.20M a year more expensive even before these items
Source: Northline Home briefing pack (synthetic case data), sections 3–5. Transport rates exclude facility cost, damage and exit charge. 2028: Eastern volume +10% to 220k.

slides.title: On an all-in basis, retaining and optimizing East (Option K) is the cheapest design in both 2027 and 2028 under the base reading of the cross-dock quote

paragraphs.text: On an all-in basis, retaining and optimizing East (Option K) is the cheapest design in both 2027 and 2028 under the base reading of the cross-dock quote
Annual all-in cost above Option K, $M

So what: K is $0.45M cheaper than the status quo over 2027–28 after its $0.15M setup cost. Both closure options cost more than K every year, and the gap widens as Eastern volume grows, because each extra Eastern order costs $3–5 more to serve.

Source: Northline Home briefing pack (synthetic case data), sections 3, 4, 6. *K's $0.30M audit saving is shown against facility cost. C excludes the unpriced carrier surcharge and the $1.1M retrofit. 2028 assumes +10% East, +6% Central, West flat.

slides.title: Closing East would beat optimized retention only if Eastern volume fell below 160k orders, against 200k in 2027 and 220k forecast for 2028

paragraphs.text: Closing East would beat optimized retention only if Eastern volume fell below 160k orders, against 200k in 2027 and 220k forecast for 2028
Annual saving of each closure option vs Option K, by Eastern volume, $M
Saving vs K = fixed cost avoided − added cost − (rate gap × Eastern orders V)
($0.30M = K's saving, lost if East closes)
A lower-growth case does not rescue closure: 2027 Eastern volume is already 200k. Volume would have to fall 20% (close to Central) or 75% (cross-dock) for closure to beat K.

Source: Northline Home briefing pack (synthetic case data), sections 3, 4, 6. Lines show the annual all-in saving vs Option K; one-time costs excluded. Assumes rates and fixed costs do not change with volume.

slides.title: THE THRESHOLD THAT MATTERS 88.3% Minimum Eastern all-ZIP two-day rate that keeps the network at 92%: (460.0k − 283.4k) ÷ 200k Close to Central (84%) is 4.3 pts short The cross-dock pilot (93%) has 4.7 pts of headroom, but on non-peak data with an unstated measurement basis (slide 10) Retaining East (96%) has 7.7 pts of headroom We ignore Finance's 98% (excludes rural ZIPs) and the online dashboard measure. Neither is the contract KPI.

paragraphs.text: Moving Eastern orders to Central would breach the contracted 92% two-day SLA; the cross-dock clears it on paper by 1.9 points
Network-wide two-day delivery rate vs the 92% contract floor, 2027, points
Minimum Eastern all-ZIP two-day rate that keeps the network at 92%: (460.0k − 283.4k) ÷ 200k
Close to Central (84%) is 4.3 pts short
The cross-dock pilot (93%) has 4.7 pts of headroom, but on non-peak data with an unstated measurement basis (slide 10)
Retaining East (96%) has 7.7 pts of headroom
We ignore Finance's 98% (excludes rural ZIPs) and the online dashboard measure. Neither is the contract KPI.
C: (168.0k + 150.4k + 133.0k) ÷ 500k = 90.3%. It needs 460k on-time orders but delivers 451k, so about 8,600 orders a year fall short, triggering retailer penalty clauses
The 84% can be lifted only with a carrier surcharge that the $13 rate does not include. Any surcharge widens C's existing $0.20M-a-year cost gap to K

Source: Northline Home briefing pack (synthetic case data), sections 2, 4. Assumes Central (94%) and West (95%) keep their current two-day rates. East's 96% is all-ZIP; the basis of the 84% (modeled) and the 93% (pilot) is not stated.

slides.title: 6% of annual Eastern volume tested 12,000 orders vs 200k a year

paragraphs.text: The cross-dock's 93% comes from a short, non-peak pilot. It needs a holiday-peak, all-ZIP test before the board relies on it
Peak weeks carry the most service risk
The quote does not say whether the 93% covers all ZIP codes
service guarantee for the national spring promotion
The operator has not committed to promotion volumes
HOW MUCH HEADROOM THE PILOT REALLY GIVES
WHAT A DECISION-GRADE TEST MUST SHOW (PROPOSED GATE CRITERIA)
Coverage: holiday peak 2027 and the spring 2028 promotion, including rural ZIPs
Service: at least 92% all-ZIP over the full test period and at least 90% in peak weeks, keeping the network at or above 93.5%
Contract: SLA defined on all ZIP codes, a termination-for-cause clause (the provider will accept this), and clarity on whether the $0.85M minimum is extra or credited
Cost: measured damage and handling rate on transshipped goods
If the pilot excluded rural ZIPs (–2 pts)*
A full-year rate is a weighted average. If peak weeks run well below the pilot, the remaining headroom of roughly 3–5 points can disappear, and the two-year contract minimum would already be signed.

Source: Northline Home briefing pack (synthetic case data), sections 4, 6, 7. *The 2-pt gap mirrors East's ex-rural (98%) vs all-ZIP (96%) difference and is illustrative only. Test thresholds are proposed by Northline analysis.

slides.title: Central would run at 100% of capacity from day one under close-to-Central and at 108% in 2028. Even a lower-growth case does not fit

paragraphs.text: Central would run at 100% of capacity from day one under close-to-Central and at 108% in 2028. Even a lower-growth case does not fit
Central hub annual shipments vs 360k certified practical capacity, thousands
WHY CAPACITY RULES OUT OPTION C
2027: 160k Central + 200k Eastern = 360k, with zero headroom for the national promotion or peaks
Any positive growth breaches capacity; only zero growth fits, and then exactly at 100%
THE FIX DOES NOT FIT THE PLAN
Operations: absorbing East at Central with today's staffing (the consultant's June 2027 plan) puts Central at full practical load before any demand spike
Expansion needs a two-quarter permit and a $1.1M retrofit that is not in the 2027 budget
Capacity is not a reason to reject the cross-dock or K, because neither adds load to Central (47% in 2028)

Source: Northline Home briefing pack (synthetic case data), sections 2, 4, 5. *Lower-growth case (half the forecast: East +5%, Central +3%) is illustrative; the pack asks for one to be discussed but does not size it.

slides.title: Retention and the deferral path fit easily within the $0.9M one-time authority; close-to-Central fits only if the $1.1M Central retrofit it needs is left unfunded

paragraphs.text: Retention and the deferral path fit easily within the $0.9M one-time authority; close-to-Central fits only if the $1.1M Central retrofit it needs is left unfunded

categories: C  Close to Central incl. retrofit

paragraphs.text: Exit in 2027 costs a one-time $0.75M; otherwise the lease expires in 2029
Waiting to 2029 avoids the early-termination fee; this is the natural point to decide
Outside this decision; West stays as-is
Fixed cost unchanged in every option; any expansion needs a permit and a $1.1M retrofit
No cost saving from adding load; expansion has to be budgeted for 2028 or later
Two-year minimum at $0.85M a year; open to a termination-for-cause clause if the SLA is all-ZIP
Signing in 2027 locks in about $1.7M of minimums before peak service is proven

Option C's $1.85M = $0.75M East exit and transfer + $1.1M Central retrofit. Without the retrofit, C leaves only $0.15M of authority for customer migration; with it, C is over budget, and a two-quarter permit means the retrofit could not be ready for a June 2027 closure.
The board's rule that service cannot be degraded to win a freight discount also limits any attempt to close C's cost gap through cheaper, slower carriers.
Source: Northline Home briefing pack (synthetic case data), sections 2, 4, 6. *The cross-dock test cap of $0.25M is a Northline assumption, pending a provider quote.

slides.title: Only optimized retention (K, alone or with the test in D) passes all five tests. The cross-dock fails on cost and is unproven on service; close-to-Central fails four tests

paragraphs.text: Only optimized retention (K, alone or with the test in D) passes all five tests. The cross-dock fails on cost and is unproven on service; close-to-Central fails four tests
Two-year minimum; nine months to reverse
+$0.20M a year vs K; $0 saving vs SQ by 2028

Read-across: K and D pass on today's evidence. D adds a cheap option on the cross-dock for the 2029 lease decision, so it is the recommended path. 'Unproven' counts as a fail until a peak test is complete.
Source: Northline Home briefing pack (synthetic case data), sections 2–7; Northline analysis (slides 6–12).

slides.title: Deferring the decision to the 2029 lease end costs little and answers the one contract question that could make the cross-dock worthwhile

paragraphs.text: Deferring the decision to the 2029 lease end costs little and answers the one contract question that could make the cross-dock worthwhile
The cross-dock quote can be read two ways, and the answer swings its economics by $0.85M a year
Reading A (base case): $0.85M minimum is a fixed fee on top of $11 per order
Never worth closing East at forecast volumes
Reading B (sensitivity): $0.85M is a spend floor, credited against the $11-per-order charges
Could be worth it if peak all-ZIP service is proven
WHY WAITING BEATS CLOSING NOW, EVEN UNDER READING B
WHAT THE DEFERRAL PATH COSTS AND BUYS
Closing in 2027 gains little: under Reading B the 2027–28 gain over K is $0.40M + $0.34M − $0.75M exit + $0.15M of K setup avoided = $0.14M over two years
Waiting avoids the early-exit fee: the lease ends in 2029, so the $0.75M termination charge falls away (any transfer costs within it may remain)
The downside is lopsided: each point of Eastern service below 88.3% adds 2,000 late orders a year and pushes the network below the 92% contract floor, with penalties and nine months to reverse
Early-exit fee avoided by waiting to 2029
Cross-dock minimums not committed before proof
Close-to-Central is dropped, not deferred: it loses to K at any volume above 160k.

Source: Northline Home briefing pack (synthetic case data), sections 3, 6, 7. Reading B is a sensitivity, not the base case: the pack lists the $0.85M under fixed facility cost. *The ≤$0.25M test cost is an assumption.

slides.title: Execute in three steps: optimize East now, test the cross-dock through peak and promotion, and take the 2029 lease decision at a Q3 2028 gate

paragraphs.text: Execute in three steps: optimize East now, test the cross-dock through peak and promotion, and take the 2029 lease decision at a Q3 2028 gate
Renegotiate East staffing shifts; set up the low-volume SKU transfer buffer
Guardrail: East all-ZIP two-day rate at or above 95%, tracked weekly
Confirm East can handle 220k orders in 2028
Negotiate a test contract: all-ZIP SLA, termination for cause, how the minimum is treated
Route a sample of Eastern orders, including rural ZIPs, through holiday 2027 and spring 2028
Measure the all-ZIP rate, peak weeks, damage and cost per order
Close East at lease end only if all four gate criteria are met
Otherwise renew East and keep optimizing
Either way, transition before the 2029 expiry
Q3 2028 GATE: CLOSE EAST AT LEASE END ONLY IF ALL FOUR HOLD
DECISIONS REQUESTED FROM THE BOARD TODAY
1  Keep East open in 2027; do not serve the East region from Central
3  Authorize a cross-dock test of up to $0.25M with an all-ZIP SLA and no two-year minimum (subject to provider agreement)
4  Schedule the 2029 lease gate for Q3 2028
≥92% all-ZIP over the test; ≥90% in peak weeks
At least $0.2M a year below K at forecast volume
All-ZIP SLA, termination for cause, budget fit

Source: Northline Home briefing pack (synthetic case data), sections 6, 7. Timing assumes the 2029 lease expiry leaves at least six months after the gate; confirm the exact expiry date. The gate thresholds are proposals.

slides.title: The recommendation holds under the main uncertainties. Each one has a monitoring trigger and a planned response

paragraphs.text: The recommendation holds under the main uncertainties. Each one has a monitoring trigger and a planned response
K's $0.30M saving does not materialize (audit estimate)
Still the right call: the status quo ($8.74M) beats the cross-dock ($8.89M), and close-to-Central fails the SLA and capacity tests regardless
Track savings quarterly; stop the shift changes if service suffers
Headroom is 7.7 pts on the Eastern rate (96% vs 88.3%)
Weekly all-ZIP tracking; act if East drops below 95%
Growth falls short (marketplace promotion not contracted)
Closure still loses: 2027 volume is already 200k, above every break-even except C vs status quo (220k)
Rerun break-evens at the Q3 2028 gate with actual volumes
East site capacity is not stated in the pack; 220k is assumed to fit
Confirm East capacity in the Q1 2027 audit
Customer retention response to service is unknown
Not used: the 92% contract floor binds regardless; Marketing's 8-pt claim is confounded
Run a controlled renewal analysis (by account size and sales coverage)
Cross-dock peak performance, damage rate and contract terms are unknown
These are exactly what the test resolves; no commitment before the gate
Matters only for close-to-Central, which is dropped
Source: Northline Home briefing pack (synthetic case data), sections 4, 5, 7; Northline analysis.
